unmatched_predictions: Proof that supports that explanation, such as ads run, campaign screenshots, marketplace listings, press coverage, or promotion emails sent to customers.
Current list of products or services actually being sold, with price ranges, to check they still match the declared business category (MCC 5399 - general merchandise).
Live website or app URL and any social media store links currently in use for accepting payments, if these have changed since onboarding.
Confirmation of whether the merchant has started selling through any new sales channel (new website, marketplace, reseller, or agent) that could explain the volume change.
GST returns or sales register extract for the recent period, to check that reported sales are consistent with the payment volumes seen.
Written confirmation that the merchant has not shared, rented, or sublet their payment account or terminals to any third party (no transaction laundering / no aggregation for others).
Details of top repeat customers or bulk buyers during the spike period, if any single buyers account for a large share of volume.
Refund and cancellation policy currently shown to customers, and confirmation it matches what was declared at onboarding.

Updated list of directors, beneficial owners, and authorised signatories, with confirmation that there has been no change in ownership or control since onboarding (and documents if there has been a change).
Confirmation of current registered and operating business address, with a recent utility bill or rent agreement if the address has changed.
Stock purchase records or supplier invoices for the spike period, to show the merchant actually had goods to sell at that scale.
Full transaction-level data for the spike period and a normal baseline period: counts, ticket sizes, timestamps, success/failure rates, and payment methods used.
Analysis of average ticket size during the spike versus the merchant's historical average, to spot sudden changes in transaction value patterns.
Time-of-day and day-of-week pattern analysis, to spot unnatural patterns (for example: transactions at odd hours, evenly spaced "robotic" transactions, or round-number amounts).
Card/customer concentration analysis: how many unique cards, UPI IDs, or customers made up the spike volume, and whether a few instruments were used repeatedly.
Geographic analysis of transactions (customer IP locations, card issuing banks, UPI handles) compared with the merchant's normal customer footprint.
Chargeback, dispute, and refund history for the account, including any disputes already raised on spike-period transactions.
Failed and declined transaction rates during the spike, since card-testing or fraud attacks often show high decline rates.
Original KYC file: certificate of incorporation, PAN, GST registration, board resolution, director KYC, and bank account proof collected at onboarding.
Onboarding-time website/app review records and declared business model, to compare against what the merchant is selling now.
Fresh screening of the merchant entity and its directors against sanctions lists, RBI caution/alert lists, negative news, and internal blocklists.
Check of whether the merchant, its directors, or its bank account are linked to any other merchant accounts on the platform (shared phone, email, address, device, or account number).
History of past risk flags, support tickets, and complaints on this account, including how earlier flags were resolved.
Terminal and device telemetry for the spike period: device IDs, IP addresses, and locations from which payments were initiated or the dashboard was accessed, checked for unusual changes.
Cybercrime and consumer complaint checks: any complaints received against this merchant through banks, NPCI, card networks, or the national cybercrime portal.

Comparison of the merchant's spike-period pattern against known fraud typologies (card testing, transaction laundering, pass-through processing, bust-out) documented in the aggregator's risk playbook.
Settlement and payout history to date, including any earlier holds, and the current amount held.
Check of whether the merchant's declared MCC and pricing plan still fit the observed transaction behaviour, based on internal MCC-monitoring rules.

unmatched_predictions: SIM/connectivity records for the device — data usage, SIM active/suspended status, and last network registration.
Full transaction history for the 6 months before dormancy — daily volume, ticket size, and the exact date and amount of the last card-present transaction.
Trend check on whether volumes tapered gradually or stopped abruptly on a single date, since an abrupt stop points to a device or premises event.
Chargeback, dispute, fraud and excessive-refund history before the stoppage, to rule out that the merchant went quiet to avoid scrutiny.
Any earlier risk alerts, holds, warnings or transaction-laundering suspicions on this MID.
Exact figure of funds currently on hold, the settlement cycle they belong to, and whether any reserve or rolling reserve is also held.
Date and destination account of the last successful settlement to this merchant.
Whether any settlement to the merchant bounced or was returned by the bank before dormancy.
Existing KYC file — proprietor PAN, Aadhaar or other officially valid document, business proof, address proof — and the date each was collected.
KYC due-date check under RBI periodic updation rules, since a 31-month-old account may be due for re-KYC anyway.
Existing bank proof on file (cancelled cheque or bank letter) and the last penny-drop or account validation result.
Existing GST registration number on file and its current status on the GST portal.
Existing FSSAI licence on file for the restaurant and its expiry date.
Existing Shop and Establishment or municipal trade licence on file and its expiry date.
Re-run of name screening against sanctions, PEP, law enforcement and card network negative lists (MATCH/VMAS) for the proprietor and the business.
Verification that the declared MCC 5812 matches the ticket sizes and transaction timing seen in the historical data, to confirm the restaurant coding was genuine.
Onboarding file check on the registered business address, geo-coordinates captured at installation, and photos taken at the time of the merchant visit.
Comparison of the terminal's last known location data against the registered address, to detect whether the device was moved elsewhere.
Confirmation of the current registered contact details on file — mobile, email, address — and whether recent communications were delivered or bounced.

A written explanation of why there were no card transactions for 94 days, with dates — for example temporary closure, renovation, seasonal shutdown, illness, family emergency, staff shortage, or a shift to UPI QR or another bank's machine.
Confirmation of whether the business is still running at the same address, and if it has moved, the new complete address.
Proof that the outlet is currently trading — recent dated photographs of the shopfront, signage, interior and the terminal in place, ideally geo-tagged.
Current premises proof — registered rent agreement, lease, or ownership document covering today's date.
A recent utility bill for the premises (electricity, water or property tax) not older than 3 months, showing continuous occupation.
Bank statements of the business current account for the last 6 to 12 months, showing whether the business kept earning through cash, UPI or another acquirer.
GST returns filed for the dormant period (GSTR-3B and GSTR-1), or a written declaration of nil filing with proof if turnover was actually nil.
Latest income tax return of the proprietor along with the computation of income for the business.
A valid and unexpired FSSAI licence, if the one on file has lapsed.
A valid and unexpired Shop and Establishment or municipal trade licence, if the one on file has lapsed.
Fresh KYC documents of the proprietor — PAN, Aadhaar or other officially valid document — if the file is due for periodic updation or the documents have expired.

A recent photograph of the proprietor and a live or video verification, to confirm the proprietor is the same person and is alive and running the business, since a proprietorship ends with the proprietor.
Confirmation that the settlement bank account is unchanged and still active, with a cancelled cheque or recent bank statement header carrying the account holder's name, account number and IFSC.
Fresh bank account details with proof, if the account has been closed, become dormant, or changed.

Confirmation of the current physical location and serial number of the terminal, with a photograph of the device label, so the aggregator knows the device was not sold, lost or handed to a third party.
A declaration that the terminal was not shared with, sub-let to, or used by any other business or person during the dormant period.
Disclosure of any other card acceptance arrangements the merchant now uses — other banks, aggregators, QR codes or aggregated UPI — with the provider names.
Confirmation of whether the nature of business, menu, or business model has changed in any way, since a change may require a different MCC.
Expected monthly card volume, average ticket size and highest expected ticket size going forward, so limits can be reset sensibly.

An undertaking that the merchant will only process genuine sales of their own restaurant business, will not process for third parties, and understands the TID may be deactivated again on prolonged inactivity.
Confirmation of current contact details — mobile number, email and person to deal with — for future alerts.
A fresh merchant site visit or verification report by the aggregator's own field team or agency, confirming the outlet is open and operating at the registered address.
Final risk sign-off record confirming the reactivation decision, the revised limits, and the release of the held settlement to the validated bank account.
